Voters delivered a thorough repudiation of Donald Trump in last week's
midterms, with Americans making clear they are desperate for financial help.

After Democrats picked up (at least) seven red Senate seats and their biggest
House majority in decades, the party believes it has a mandate for its
"affordability" agenda. What is that agenda exactly? So far, the party's pitch
seems to be attempting a return to the pre-Trump economic status quo that saw
him get elected for a second time - and don't you _dare_ demand structural
changes.

Who knows what will be said, of course, at the "What's Next 2026" conference
put on later this week by Majority Democrats - part of the [billionaire-funded
network](https://www.levernews.com/the-new-democratic-machine-and-the-
billionaires-behind-it/) that backed [some of the
moderates](https://www.thebench.org/candidates/) who won Democrats' most
consequential midterm victories. But the Majority Democrats who went on TV on
Sunday made clear the moderates are eager and ready to punch left, and don't
have big policies in mind.

Americans certainly delivered a message about affordability last Tuesday. In
[NBC exit polls](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-elections/exit-polls),
75% of voters gave the economy a negative rating, with 59% saying they're very
concerned about the costs of gas and groceries and healthcare. Voters
delivered a message about affordability when they elected Trump again, too -
they [were mad](https://www.rollingstone.com/politics/politics-features/why-
kamala-harris-lost-election-2024-1235154713/) about the brutal economy before
Trump's disastrous Iran war, tariffs, and healthcare cuts.

It's been less than a week since Democrats won the midterms so it is perhaps
unfair to expect Democrats to have offered a full-fledged policy agenda by now
- though they could have easily campaigned on one. There is obviously a large,
Trump-sized impediment to what Democrats can expect to accomplish once they
take full control of Congress next year. The president will surely attempt to
set the agenda and steer the discourse each day, even if Americans despise
him.

What we're seeing already from liberal influencers and Democrats, well before
they're sworn in, feels sadly familiar: a half-hearted pledge to solve _some_
problems _part-way_ , buttressed with assertions that this is exactly what
Americans voted for - indeed, the only politically responsible way.

As Neera Tanden, a former Joe Biden adviser who leads the Center for American
Progress, [put it](https://x.com/ClippingWings/status/2119863945318048212) in
a speech on Monday, "The next two years should not be an opportunity for every
organization or group in DC to dust off their wish list for the last decade…
It is time to ensure, and relentlessly ensure, we deliver for the voters who
just trusted us."

The big question for Democrats - particularly those in its moderate flank -
remains what it has been: What's their plan to actually make life in America
more affordable? And then how would they pass it?

### 'Access to Basic Levels of Healthcare'

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, the likely Democratic speaker come
January, [has](https://apnews.com/article/midterm-elections-democrats-
affordability-corruption-018019529b14a6b3bc4a343a4e17c44f)
[spoken](https://jeffries.house.gov/2026/10/14/leader-jeffries-on-ms-now-were-
going-to-relentlessly-focus-on-our-affordability-agenda/) of prioritizing
reversing several Trump administration policies: ending Trump's gas-price-
spiking war with Iran; ending his arbitrary tariffs and trade wars;
eliminating his Medicaid cuts, which are about to make [millions of people
uninsured](https://www.nbcnews.com/health/health-care/5-healthcare-fights-
democrats-take-midterms-sweep-rcna607457); reauthorizing the health insurance
subsidies that Trump let expire, cutting off insurance [for
millions](https://www.cbpp.org/research/health/health-coverage-tracker-
millions-of-people-are-losing-coverage-following-2025) on Obamacare while
spiking premiums for many more.

Enacting all of these changes is absolutely necessary. But if Democrats manage
to force those changes through now with Trump as president, they ultimately
would be delivering a return to the Biden-era economy that voters rejected.

What's the plan to make life _more_ affordable than it was under Joe Biden?

"The agenda that I've seen so far presented is not going to cut it,"
progressive Colorado Rep.-elect Melat Kiros
[told](https://www.politico.com/newsletters/playbook/2026/11/09/between-the-
bloc-and-a-hard-place-01156208) _Politico_ on Monday.

Take healthcare. Nearly six-in-ten voters
[said](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-elections/exit-polls) in midterm
exit polls that they're very concerned about the cost of healthcare when it
comes to their own financial situation; 61% said the government should play a
bigger role in helping Americans get healthcare; and 55% said the Trump
administration's policies have made their healthcare costs worse.

In 2024, before Trump's cuts to Medicaid and Obamacare, roughly 8% of
Americans [were uninsured](https://ccf.georgetown.edu/2025/09/09/us-uninsured-
rate-stays-level-in-2024-for-adults-and-kids-storm-clouds-lie-ahead/). The
U.S. was already [spending far
more](https://www.commonwealthfund.org/publications/fund-
reports/2024/sep/mirror-mirror-2024) than other wealthy countries on
healthcare, only for Americans to see worse access, worse outcomes, and
greater administrative inefficiency. It has been this way [for many
years](https://www.commonwealthfund.org/sites/default/files/documents/___media_files_publications_fund_report_2006_apr_mirror__mirror_on_the_wall__an_update_on_the_quality_of_american_health_care_through_the_patients_le_davis_mirrormirror_915_pdf.pdf).
America's healthcare system is an outlier globally, in terms of how expensive
and bad it is.

agenda?utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email&utm_content=share&action=share)

Senator-elect and pastor Adam Hamilton ran one of the more satisfying
Democratic campaigns this year in Kansas, flipping a seat Dems haven't won
since 1932. Anger with Trump played a big role, to be sure, and Hamilton is an
outstanding speaker, but he also righteously dismantled GOP Senator Roger
Marshall, an OBGYN, for suing [hundreds of
patients](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/08/us/politics/roger-marshall-obgyn-
doctor-debts.html) over medical debts.

"We've got to figure out a better way so that every person in America has
access to basic levels of healthcare," Hamilton
[said](https://x.com/atrupar/status/2113344474977849385) during a debate with
Marshall, "so that they can afford to pay for their treatment - and they
aren't being sued by their doctors when they don't get paid."

Hamilton's campaign [platform](https://hamiltonforkansas.com/issues/) includes
several important healthcare proposals outside of reversing Trump's healthcare
cuts, such as allowing Medicare to negotiate lower prices on more drugs
(including for private plans), and ending [the
scam](https://www.levernews.com/the-20-billion-scam-at-the-heart-of-medicare-
advantage/) that has the government provide massive overpayments each year to
private Medicare Advantage insurers. He wants to "reform prior authorization
so insurance paperwork cannot delay or deny care."

But there's a glaring omission among Hamilton's healthcare proposals: There is
no plan to guarantee healthcare for every American.

Speaking on CNN's 'State of the Union' on Sunday, Hamilton [said
again](https://transcripts.cnn.com/show/sotu/date/2026-11-08/segment/01) he
wants to ensure "affordable healthcare for everyone," while reiterating his
opposition to Medicare for All - arguing that insurance-industry jobs are too
important, and that the idea might sound frighteningly European to voters in
Kansas.

"I think there are people who worry, what does that look like?" he
[said](https://x.com/CNNSOTU/status/2119458288718708985). "They have a sense
of Europe and other places, where they're not certain this is - I mean, there
are places in Europe people love their healthcare, but there are other places
where people complain about the length of time it takes to be able to get
treatment. Who's approving treatment, I think people are a bit antsy about
that."

Access to care is, of course,
[better](https://www.commonwealthfund.org/publications/fund-
reports/2024/sep/mirror-mirror-2024) in Europe. Per exit
[polls](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-elections/kansas-senate-
results#exit-polls), 60% of voters in Kansas are very concerned about
healthcare costs, and 56% believe the government should do more to help
Americans get care.

### 'We Cannot Make the Same Mistake'

So what reforms do _other_ moderate Democrats propose to meaningfully lower
costs and ensure every American has healthcare coverage?

When I tweeted
[something](https://x.com/andrewperezdc/status/2119513303613653245) similar
Sunday, Rohan Patel, executive director of Majority Democrats,
[replied](https://x.com/rohanspatel/status/2119515134875906496) with a video
his organization released last month pitching a plan called "Medicare for
Americans."

This is their derivative name for their version of a public health insurance
option - something Democrats have been advocating for since at least 2008.

You may remember Barack Obama pushed for a public option during the Affordable
Care Act debate, [before dropping it](https://zeteo.com/p/ill-try-to-be-less-
of-an-idiot-read). Joe Biden called for a public option during the 2020
campaign, as a counter to Bernie Sanders's Medicare-for-All proposal. Biden
[never once mentioned it](https://www.levernews.com/where-did-the-public-
option-go/) as president.

There are benefits to Medicare for All from a policy perspective. Everyone
would have coverage. Making the government the single payer (instead of having
a patchwork of payers) would allow it to negotiate lower prices. It would
eliminate a ton of administrative bloat. Medicare for All [would save
money](https://zeteo.com/p/i-believed-american-healthcare-was), despite the
heavy price tag its critics attach to it.

Moderates would tell you there are political benefits to supporting a public-
option plan like "Medicare for Americans." [Their primary
argument](https://zeteo.com/p/medicare-for-all-poll-searchlight-institute) is
that Americans don't want to change their health insurance plans or lose the
coverage they receive through their employers.

There are a few cons as well. A public option is unlikely to save as much
money as Medicare for All - the plan would not have the same leverage over
providers and drug companies as one, single government payer. It would not
necessarily guarantee universal coverage.

Another problem: The insurance, drug, and hospital industries would work just
as hard and spend as much money to kill a public option as they would Medicare
for All, as [past experience
shows](https://theintercept.com/2019/08/06/business-group-spending-on-
lobbying-in-washington-is-at-least-double-whats-publicly-reported/). And
they'll [argue](https://americashealthcarefuture.org/proposals/) that a public
option would be every bit as radical and destructive as Medicare for All.

Perhaps the biggest issue? Based on the history of the public option to date,
does anyone believe moderate Democrats would _actually_ try to pass it? Or is
the public option just a useful talking point to try to shut down conversation
around Medicare for All?

It's hard not to notice the Majority Democrats' video pitching "Medicare for
Americans" spends much of its run-time dumping on Medicare for All.

When Majority Democrats adviser Lis Smith, [formerly an
aide](https://www.washingtonpost.com/opinions/2022/07/22/lis-smith-book-
andrew-cuomo-discrepancies/) to disgraced ex-Governor Andrew Cuomo of New
York, [appeared](https://abcnews.com/Politics/week-transcript-11-8-26-house-
democratic-leader/story?id=137944448) on ABC's 'This Week' [on
Sunday](https://x.com/MajorityDems/status/2119472753862431168), she did not
bother touting her group's public-option plan.

Smith - who helped lead Pete Buttigieg's 2020 campaign promoting "Medicare for
All Who Want It" - instead laid into Medicare for All, complaining that some
progressives hope Democrats will win even more seats in 2028 so that they can
implement it.

"I support celebrating this election. I do not support this irrational
exuberance," she said, comparing it to how Trump and Republicans thought they
had a "mandate" to unleash violent ICE agents on U.S. cities and communities.

"We cannot make the same mistake," she said, continuing: "The majority of
Democrats did not run on Medicare for All. You think Adam Hamilton… got
elected in Kansas by saying: _I want to kick everyone off their private
insurance_?"

"I support expanding healthcare, but let's be real about that," Smith added.

### A Story We've Heard Before

Healthcare policy is just one critical component of any "affordability" agenda
- but it tends to reveal a politician's commitment to acknowledging big
problems, and thus doing what's necessary to solve them.

The same goes with Democrats' position on the Senate filibuster, which
requires 60 votes to pass most legislation. The filibuster [can
end](https://www.brookings.edu/articles/what-is-the-senate-filibuster-and-
what-would-it-take-to-eliminate-it/) with a simple majority vote; if Senate
Democrats keep it in place, they would ensure they can't pass much of an
"affordability" agenda at all - beyond trying to reverse some of Trump's
damage, such as his Medicaid and Obamacare cuts.

Time and time again, moderate Democrats' commitment to maintaining the Senate
filibuster and other procedural norms has been used to curtail the party's
supposed core priorities - from killing [the public option under
Obama](https://zeteo.com/p/ill-try-to-be-less-of-an-idiot-read), to blocking a
long-promised [minimum wage hike](https://www.levernews.com/lessons-from-
todays-doomed-effort/) under Biden, to snuffing out Dems'
[effort](https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/senate-parliamentarian-
approves-most-drug-price-controls-in-democrats-economic-package) to force drug
companies to charge private insurance plans the same lower prices negotiated
by Medicare.

[Share](https://zeteo.com/p/democrats-affordability-
agenda?utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email&utm_content=share&action=share)

And the current crop of moderate Dems [doesn't seem
keen](https://x.com/theodoricmeyer/status/2050208894211797214?s=20) to remove
their legislative block.

"I don't think we should end the filibuster," Hamilton
[said](https://www.washingtonexaminer.com/news/senate/4795084/john-fetterman-
filibuster-backup-new-senate-democrats/) last month on Fox. "I'm not going to
vote for that."

Trump's favorite Democratic senator, Israel fanatic John Fetterman, is [pro-
filibuster](https://www.washingtonpost.com/opinions/2026/07/27/john-fetterman-
why-i-changed-my-mind-about-filibuster/) now. Maine Senator Angus King, an
independent who caucuses with Democrats, has similarly [changed his
mind](https://x.com/theodoricmeyer/status/2050208894211797214?s=20) and wants
to preserve the filibuster, too.

Senators-elect Chris Pappas of New Hampshire and Josh Turek of Iowa, two more
incoming Senate moderates, have
[expressed](https://www.iowapbs.org/shows/iowapress/special/14067/iowa-press-
debates-us-senate-democratic-primary#show-transcript)
[support](https://www.semafor.com/article/06/26/2026/new-hampshire-becomes-
the-senate-midterms-sleeper-race) for modifying filibuster rules without
getting rid of it.

The 2026 midterm results can only be seen as a massive win for democracy, as
Americans rejected Trump and established a check on his authoritarian
presidency, while once again pleading for financial help from Washington.

Unfortunately, it's not clear that Democrats have a plan to make life more
affordable for Americans than it was under Biden. And if they did, it's not
clear that they would allow themselves to pass it.

We all know how this story ends - and that's why the real fight starts now.
